title: Numerical Optimization for Statistics
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter answers a practical question: when a function you need to minimize (usually a negative log-likelihood or a loss) has no closed-form minimizer, how do you find one numerically, and which of the many available strategies should you reach for? It covers univariate and multivariate optimization, how to tell whether an iterative method is actually converging, the two big families of algorithms that recur across statistics (Newton-type methods and derivative-free methods), what convexity buys you, and how constraints change the picture. It assumes single- and multivariable calculus (gradients, Hessians, Taylor expansions), enough linear algebra to be comfortable with positive definiteness, eigenvalues, and the QR/SVD decompositions, and enough statistics to know what a likelihood, an MLE, and a GLM are. ## Setting up the problem Optimization shows up whenever a model can't be fit in closed form: finding the MLE for a GLM, fitting a nonlinear regression model $Y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(g(z_i;\beta),\sigma^2)$ for nonlinear $g$, maximizing a likelihood subject to constraints, or fitting a machine learning model. We always talk about *minimization*, since maximizing $f$ is the same as minimizing $-f$. The problem is to find $$x^{*}=\arg\min_{x\in D}f(x),$$ where $D$ is the domain. When $D=\mathbb{R}^p$ this is *unconstrained* optimization; otherwise the constraints on $x$ have to be handled explicitly (the last section of this chapter). We'll assume $f$ is continuous throughout — there's little that can be done systematically otherwise. For a differentiable function, minimizing in one dimension is the same problem as finding a root of the derivative: a minimum can only occur where $f'(x^{*})=0$, and it genuinely is a local minimum provided $f''(x^{*})\ge 0$. In more than one dimension the analogous condition is that the Hessian at $x^{*}$ is positive semi-definite — moving away from $x^{*}$ in *any* direction doesn't take you downhill. Different strategies suit a discrete, countable domain (as arises in variable selection) versus a continuous, dense one; this chapter concentrates on the continuous case. **Notation used throughout.** For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_p)$, the gradient is the column vector of first partial derivatives, $$f'(x)=\nabla f(x)=\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1},\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_p}\right)^\top,$$ and the Hessian is the matrix of second partials, $$f''(x)=\nabla^2 f(x) = H_f(x) = \left(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}\right)_{i,j=1}^p.$$ Iterative algorithms produce a sequence $x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_t, x_{t+1}$ converging (we hope) to $x^{*}$; $x_0$ is a starting point that must be chosen, often carefully. $x$ (or $\theta$, when talking explicitly about a likelihood) denotes the argument being optimized, $Y$ denotes data, and $z$ denotes covariates, kept visually distinct from $x$. Optimization is, to a first approximation, a solved problem with good general-purpose software — but the function being optimized changes with every problem and can be genuinely tricky, so it's worth knowing the menu of strategies, their failure modes, and how to choose among them. Finding a *global* rather than merely *local* minimum is a persistent extra difficulty. (MCMC-based methods for optimization, such as simulated annealing's cousins in a Bayesian context, are mentioned only in passing below.) ## Univariate optimization Methods for optimizing a function of one variable matter beyond the univariate case itself, because multivariate algorithms repeatedly fall back on a univariate *line search* as a subroutine. ### Bracketing methods: golden section and bisection **Golden section search** requires only that $f$ be *unimodal* — a single minimum on an interval $[a,b]$. Evaluate $f$ at two interior points $x_1 < x_2$; whichever sub-interval the larger value lies in cannot contain the minimum's interior, so it is discarded (the standard case: $f(x_1) < f(x_2)$ discards $[x_2, b]$). A third point is placed in what remains using the golden ratio $\phi$, chosen so that $\phi - \phi^2 = 2\phi - 1$ — this is exactly the condition that keeps the *proportions* of the new sub-intervals consistent with the old ones, so every iteration shrinks the bracket by the same factor $1-\phi \approx 0.382$, regardless of $f$. Once $|x_t - x_{t-1}|$ is below tolerance, report $(x_t+x_{t-1})/2$. No derivative is needed. **Bisection** needs $f'$ to exist and be evaluable, and still assumes unimodality, but shrinks the bracket faster. Start with an interval $(a_0,b_0)$ and $x_0$ its midpoint. At step $t$, with current interval $[a_t,b_t]$: - if $f'(a_t)f'(x_t) < 0$, the derivative changes sign between $a_t$ and $x_t$, so (by the intermediate value theorem) the root — the minimum — lies in $[a_t, x_t]$; - if $f'(a_t)f'(x_t) > 0$, it lies in $[x_t, b_t]$ instead; and $x_{t+1}$ is the midpoint of the new interval. Because bisection halves the bracket each step ($0.5 > 0.382$), it needs fewer iterations per digit of accuracy than golden section (roughly 3–4 iterations per decimal digit) — the price of using derivative information. Both methods are *bracketing* methods: they trap the minimum inside a shrinking, nested sequence of intervals. That makes them slow but robust, and (for bisection) they don't require a second derivative to exist. ### Newton–Raphson Newton–Raphson (N–R) is usually introduced as root-finding, but as an optimization method it is the same algorithm viewed as finding a root of $f'$. It needs two continuous derivatives, buys speed in exchange, and still assumes unimodality (more precisely: convergence to *a* critical point, not necessarily *the* minimum — see below). Near a current guess $x_0$, Taylor-expand $$f'(x) \approx f'(x_0) + (x-x_0)f''(x_0),$$ set the left side to zero (the condition satisfied at $x^{*}$), and solve for $x$: $$x_1 = x_0 - \frac{f'(x_0)}{f''(x_0)}, \qquad\text{iterating}\qquad x_{t+1} = x_t - \frac{f'(x_t)}{f''(x_t)}.$$ Geometrically, this is following the tangent line to $f'$ at $x_t$ down to where it crosses zero — equivalently, finding the exact minimum of the quadratic Taylor approximation to $f$ at $x_t$. If $f'$ is twice continuously differentiable, convex, and has a root, N–R converges from *any* starting point — a strong hypothesis, and one that fails often enough that the failure modes below are worth knowing. **Secant variant.** To avoid computing $f''$ analytically, approximate it by the secant slope of $f'$ through the last two iterates, $$f''(x_t) \approx \frac{f'(x_t)-f'(x_{t-1})}{x_t - x_{t-1}},$$ which needs two starting points $x_0, x_1$. A symmetric finite-difference approximation, $f''(x_t) \approx \big(f'(x_t+h)-f'(x_t-h)\big)/(2h)$, is a common alternative. ### How Newton's method goes wrong There are three distinct ways $f(x_{t+1}) > f(x_t)$ can happen, worth holding on to as a checklist: 1. **Ordinary overshoot** in a region where $f$ is fairly flat. 2. **Divergence**, when $f''(x_t)$ is small: dividing by a small second derivative produces a huge step, sending $x_{t+1}$ far from $x_t$ (though still in the correct direction). Repeated, this can send the iterates to numerical overflow and then NaN. With $f'(x)$ the logistic-type function $e^{\theta x}/(1+e^{\theta x}) - 0.5$, starting at $x_0=1$ or $x_0=2$ converges quickly, but $x_0=2.5$ diverges. 3. **Climbing uphill**, when $f''(x_t) < 0$: N–R finds *a* critical point, not necessarily a minimum, so it can walk to a local *maximum* instead. Minimizing $\cos(x)$ (minimum at $x^{*}\approx\pi$), starting from $x_0=5.5$ walks uphill to a local maximum, since the second derivative there is negative; starting from $x_0=4.3$ nearly diverges before recovering, and $x_0=3.8$ converges cleanly — three quite different outcomes from nearby starting points. **Making it more robust.** One general fix is to *safeguard* the fast-but-fragile N–R step with a slow-but-robust bracketing method: track the bracket implied by the derivative evaluations seen so far, and if the proposed N–R step would leave it, take a bisection step instead. A second fix is *backtracking*: if a proposed step increases $f$, shrink it (repeated halving is the crudest option) until it decreases $f$, or fit a polynomial to the known values $f(x_{t+1})$, $f(x_t)$, $f'(x_t)$, $f''(x_t)$ and step to that polynomial's minimum. A full line search at every N–R step is usually not worth the extra computation, since the next iteration heads off in a new direction anyway. ## Judging convergence ### Convergence metrics Checking whether $f'(x_t)$ is near zero is tempting but unreliable: on a flat part of the domain, the derivative can be near zero far from the optimum. So software generally monitors how much $x$ itself is still moving instead. **Absolute convergence**: $|x_{t+1}-x_t| < \epsilon$. **Relative convergence**: $|x_{t+1}-x_t|/|x_t| < \epsilon$, which accounts for the scale of $x$ but needs guarding near $x_t=0$, e.g. $|x_{t+1}-x_t|/(|x_t|+\epsilon) < \epsilon$. Choose $\epsilon$ with machine precision in mind — for relative convergence, the square root of machine epsilon (about $10^{-8}$) is a reasonable default. For multivariate $x$, replace the scalar difference with a norm $\|x_{t+1}-x_t\|_p$, usually $p=1$ or $2$. An algorithm that hits its iteration cap without meeting the criterion, or whose convergence measure plateaus or oscillates, has *failed to converge* — sometimes it just needs more iterations, but often this is a signal that something is wrong with the objective or the starting value. ### Starting values and multimodality Good starting values matter for three separate reasons: speed, avoiding divergence or cycling, and avoiding a local (rather than global) optimum. Multiple or randomized starting values are the standard defense against multimodality. A classic torture-test function for this is the **Rastrigin function**, $$f(x) = An + \sum_{i=1}^n \big(x_i^2 - A\cos(2\pi x_i)\big),$$ which has many local optima whatever $n$ is, and is considered genuinely hard to optimize once $n$ reaches something like 30. ### Order of convergence Let $\epsilon_t = |x_t - x^{*}|$. If $$\lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{|\epsilon_{t+1}|}{|\epsilon_t|^{\beta}} = c$$ exists for some $\beta>0$ and $c\ne 0$, the method has **order of convergence** $\beta$: roughly, $|\epsilon_{t+1}| \approx c|\epsilon_t|^{\beta}$. Bisection, though it doesn't strictly satisfy the hypotheses of this definition, behaves roughly like **linear convergence** ($\beta=1$): the error shrinks by a constant factor each step. Newton–Raphson has **quadratic convergence** ($\beta=2$), which is what makes it fast. To see why: Taylor-expand $f'(x^{*})$ around $x_t$ to third order, $$f'(x^{*}) = f'(x_t) + (x^{*}-x_t)f''(x_t) + \tfrac12(x^{*}-x_t)^2 f'''(\xi_t) = 0$$ for some $\xi_t$ between $x^{*}$ and $x_t$. Substituting the N–R update and rearranging gives $$\frac{|\epsilon_{t+1}|}{|\epsilon_t|^{2}} = \left|\frac{1}{2}\frac{f'''(\xi_t)}{f''(x_t)}\right|,$$ and as $x_t \to x^{*}$ (given twice continuous differentiability) this tends to $c = \left|\tfrac12 f'''(x^{*})/f''(x^{*})\right|$, confirming $\beta=2$. If $c=1$, $k$ correct digits at step $t$ become $2k$ correct digits at step $t+1$ (e.g. $\epsilon_t=0.01$ gives $\epsilon_{t+1}=0.0001$) — this is exactly what "quadratic convergence is fast" means numerically. A smaller $c$ is better, so a large second derivative and a small third derivative both help; the formula also shows the method breaks down precisely where $f''(x_t)=0$ — visibly the point at which the tangent line in the picture above goes horizontal and the update blows up. The secant-based variant of N–R, which approximates $f''$ by a finite difference, has order of convergence about $1.62$ (Givens and Hoeting) — between linear and quadratic. ## Multivariate optimization Higher dimension brings genuinely new difficulties: many more directions to search in each step, calculations involving large vectors and matrices, and multimodality that is both more common and harder to detect. ### Profiling When part of the parameter vector can be maximized *analytically*, do that first: if $\theta = (\theta_1,\theta_2)$ and $\theta_2$ can be maximized in closed form given $\theta_1$, substituting the resulting $\hat\theta_2(\theta_1)$ back into the objective gives a **profile** objective in $\theta_1$ alone, over which numerical optimization is much simpler. Example: for regression with correlated errors, $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(X\beta, \sigma^2\Sigma(\rho))$, the maximum over $\beta$ given $\rho$ is the GLS estimator $\hat\beta(\rho) = (X^\top\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}X)^{-1}X^\top\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}Y$; the maximum over $\sigma^2$ given $\rho$ is then also available in closed form, $$\hat\sigma^2(\rho) = \frac{(Y-X\hat\beta(\rho))^\top\Sigma(\rho)^{-1}(Y-X\hat\beta(\rho))}{n},$$ leaving a profile likelihood that is a function of the scalar $\rho$ only. ### Multivariate Newton–Raphson The multivariate update is $$x_{t+1} = x_t - H_f(x_t)^{-1}\nabla f(x_t).$$ **Worked example: Mauna Loa CO$_2$.** Fit $Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1\exp(t_i/\beta_2) + \epsilon_i$ to the annual-mean CO$_2$ record. Practical steps: center the year covariate for numerical stability; get starting values by *guessing* an order of magnitude for $\beta_2$, which makes the model linear in $(\beta_0,\beta_1)$ given that guess, and fitting those two by OLS — trying guesses of 10, 100, and 50 for $\beta_2$ and checking the resulting fit visually is enough to narrow it down; use automatic differentiation (JAX here; PyTorch or TensorFlow are alternatives) rather than hand deriving the gradient and Hessian; and check the Hessian's eigenvalues at the starting value *before* trusting an N–R step, since it need not be positive definite (it wasn't, at $\beta_2=10$ or $100$, but was at $\beta_2=50$). Given a positive-definite start, iterating $x_{t+1}=x_t-H^{-1}\nabla f$ and checking the loss decreases (raising an error if positive definiteness is lost along the way) converges to a good-looking fit — but the sensitivity to the starting value is itself a warning to be cautious about the result. In general, the three things to watch with N–R are good starting values, positive definiteness of the Hessian, and correctness of hand-derived derivatives — all reasons to reach for automatic differentiation when it's available. ### Fisher scoring The **Fisher information** is $I(\theta) = E_f\big(\nabla f(y)\nabla f(y)^\top\big)$, an expectation over the data distribution; under regularity conditions (true for exponential families), $E_f H_f(y) = -I(\theta)$. Ordinary N–R can therefore be read as using the *observed* Fisher information (the Hessian at the actual data) in place of the Hessian; using the *expected* Fisher information instead gives **Fisher scoring** (FS), $$\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t + I(\theta_t)^{-1}\nabla f(\theta_t).$$ FS and N–R share quadratic convergence; per Givens and Hoeting, FS tends to make faster early progress and N–R does better at final refinement. The Gauss–Newton algorithm for nonlinear least squares (used by R's `nls()`) is FS applied to that setting. **Ill-conditioning and statistical uncertainty are the same phenomenon.** When the observed or expected Fisher information is nearly singular, some direction in parameter space has a small eigenvalue in the *precision* — equivalently, a large-variance direction, in which the likelihood is nearly flat. Since N–R (and FS) slow down exactly where the gradient is shallow, poor numerical convergence and high statistical uncertainty go hand in hand; nearly collinear regressors are one common cause. ### IRLS for GLMs Exponential families have the form $f(y;\theta,\phi) = \exp\big((y\theta - b(\theta))/a(\phi) + c(y,\phi)\big)$ with $E(Y)=b'(\theta)$, $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=b''(\theta)$. For a GLM in canonical form ($\eta=\theta=X\beta$), the log-likelihood gradient is $(Y-E(Y))^\top X$ and the Hessian is $-X^\top WX$, where $W=\mathrm{diag}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)\}$ (the *working weights*, themselves functions of $\beta$). The N–R update is $$\beta_{t+1} = \beta_t + (X^\top W_t X)^{-1}X^\top(Y-E(Y)_t),$$ which rearranges into the weighted-least-squares form $\beta_{t+1} = (X^\top W_t X)^{-1}X^\top W_t \tilde{Y}_t$ with **working observations** $\tilde Y_t = X\beta_t + W_t^{-1}(Y-E(Y)_t)$ — the current fitted values plus a residual rescaled to the linear-predictor scale. This is **iteratively reweighted least squares** (IRLS/IWLS), the standard GLM-fitting algorithm. Because the canonical-link Hessian doesn't depend on the data, the observed and expected Fisher information coincide there, so N–R and Fisher scoring are literally the same algorithm in this case; IRLS is itself a special case of Gauss–Newton. ### Descent and Newton-like methods, generally A Newton-*like* update has the form $$x_{t+1} = x_t - \alpha_t M_t^{-1} f'(x_t),$$ and the choice of $M_t$ (some approximation to the Hessian) and step scale $\alpha_t$ opens up a family of methods addressing: cheaper approximations to the second derivative; avoiding steps that go uphill; and controlling how far each step travels. **Steepest descent.** Set $M_t=I$: move directly along $-f'(x_t)$, the direction of steepest decrease, scaled by a step length $\alpha_t$ chosen (e.g. by a line search) to ensure descent: $$x_{t+1} = x_t - \alpha_t f'(x_t).$$ On elongated (elliptical) contours, this **zigzags** badly — even with a *full* line search at every step, the path bounces back and forth across the narrow axis of the valley instead of heading toward the center. On *circular* contours, steepest descent works well; Newton's method effectively reshapes elliptical contours into circular ones using the Hessian, which is the sense in which it accounts for how the gradient itself is changing while steepest descent does not. Formally, a Taylor expansion of $f(x_{t+1})-f(x_t)$ shows the general descent step is guaranteed to decrease $f$, for small enough $\alpha_t$, whenever $M_t$ is positive definite — but positive-definite $M_t$ plus backtracking alone does not *guarantee* convergence; the steps also need to decrease $f$ quickly enough and avoid traveling along a level set. (The conjugate gradient method, also used for solving large linear systems, chooses both direction and step length with this in mind.) **Quasi-Newton methods (BFGS).** When the true Hessian is expensive, replace it with an approximation $M_t$ updated at each step using $M_t$ itself plus the curvature information revealed by the step just taken. The basic requirement is the **secant condition**, $$M_{t+1}(x_{t+1}-x_t) = \nabla f(x_{t+1}) - \nabla f(x_t),$$ motivated by the fact that the secant line approximates the change in gradient along the direction just traveled. With $s_t=x_{t+1}-x_t$, $y_t=\nabla f(x_{t+1})-\nabla f(x_t)$, the unique symmetric rank-one update satisfying the secant condition is $$M_{t+1} = M_t + \frac{(y_t-M_ts_t)(y_t-M_ts_t)^\top}{(y_t-M_ts_t)^\top s_t},$$ which is not guaranteed to be positive definite unless the denominator is treated carefully. The standard **BFGS** update (Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno) is a rank-two update that generally preserves positive definiteness, $$M_{t+1} = M_t - \frac{M_ts_t(M_ts_t)^\top}{s_t^\top M_t s_t} + \frac{y_ty_t^\top}{s_t^\top y_t},$$ and is one of the methods behind R's `optim()`. (There is also a way to update the Cholesky factor of $M_t$ directly, which is numerically preferable to updating $M_t^{-1}$.) Quasi-Newton methods converge faster than linearly but generally slower than N–R's quadratic rate, and do best when the components of $x$ are on comparable scales; Lange suggests using the expected information at a plausible starting point to seed $M_0$. One caution: don't reuse the final $M_t$ as a stand-in for the true Hessian when estimating standard errors — recompute the Hessian directly at $x^{*}$. **Stochastic gradient descent (SGD).** Ordinary gradient descent drops the second-derivative term from the Newton-like recipe but keeps the exact gradient, $x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t f'(x_t)$. SGD replaces the exact gradient with something whose *expectation* is the gradient, $E(g(x_t))=f'(x_t)$: $x_{t+1}=x_t-\alpha_t g(x_t)$ — on average still headed downhill, and SGD provably converges for convex $f$. The setting to have in mind is $f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)$, so that computing the exact gradient is $O(n)$ and may be too expensive at every step; instead, estimate it from a single randomly chosen observation, or (better, since it uses vectorized computation) from a random mini-batch. Cycling through the data in its stored order can bias the gradient badly if the data have any structure, so data are shuffled before starting SGD. It's standard to divide the objective (and gradient) by $n$ so that the expected estimated gradient equals the true gradient, independent of batch size. The step size $\alpha_t$ ("learning rate") should shrink over time — otherwise the iterate bounces around near the optimum without settling. Schedules used in practice include $\alpha_t=1/t$; a piecewise-constant schedule that multiplies by some $\gamma\in(0.8,0.9)$ every $T$ iterations; or halving $\alpha$ every time the iteration budget doubles. ### Coordinate descent (Gauss–Seidel) Also called *back-fitting*. Instead of choosing a full $p$-dimensional direction, cycle through the coordinates of $x$ one at a time: treat the $j$-th component of $f'(x)$ as a univariate function of $x_j$ alone (holding the rest fixed) and root-find/minimize it, then move to the next coordinate. One pass through all $p$ coordinates is a *cycle*; iterate cycles to convergence. This is attractive because univariate optimization is easy, stable, and fast — but coordinate descent zigzags too, for the same underlying reason steepest descent does: only one direction is available at each step. Back-fitting historically fit additive models $E(Y)=f_1(z_1)+\cdots+f_p(z_p)$ this way. **Worked example: the lasso.** Minimize $\|Y-X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|$ for a given $\lambda$. Coordinate descent (cyclic, or greedily choosing the coordinate whose directional derivative decreases the objective most) is the standard solver. Because the penalty isn't differentiable at $\beta_j=0$, work with directional derivatives: $$-2\sum_i x_{ij}(Y_i - X_i^\top\beta) \pm \lambda,$$ adding $\lambda$ if $\beta_j\ge0$ and subtracting if $\beta_j<0$ — so at $\beta_j=0$, a step in *either* direction contributes $+\lambda$ from the penalty. Having chosen a coordinate, set its directional derivative to zero and solve for the updated $\beta_j$. The `glmnet` package implements this for a range of penalties and GLMs; specialized versions (e.g. for survival analysis with very large $p$) exploit sparsity in $X$ and avoid Newton–Raphson entirely, because the matrix operations it would need become infeasible at that scale. A useful trick is **warm starts**: start from a large $\lambda$ where every coefficient is exactly zero, decrease $\lambda$, and use each fit as the starting value for the next, smaller $\lambda$ — the resulting **solution path** is what's typically combined with cross-validation to choose $\lambda$ (LARS computes a related path all at once). The lasso can equivalently be written as constrained minimization of $\|Y-X\beta\|_2^2$ subject to $\sum_j|\beta_j|\le c$ — a quadratic program, discussed under constrained optimization below. ### Nelder–Mead A derivative-free method: robust, but slower than Newton-like methods. It maintains a **simplex** of $p+1$ points in $\mathbb{R}^p$ (a triangle in 2D, a tetrahedron in 3D, …) and moves it by reflecting, expanding, contracting, or shrinking, based only on function values at the vertices. Four tuning constants: reflection $\alpha>0$, expansion $\gamma>1$, contraction $0<\beta<1$, shrinkage $0<\delta<1$. 1. Order the vertices $x_1,\ldots,x_{p+1}$ so $f(x_1)\le\cdots\le f(x_{p+1})$; let $\bar x$ be the mean of the $p$ best points. 2. **Reflect** the worst point through the hyperplane of the others: $x_r = (1+\alpha)\bar x - \alpha x_{p+1}$. 3. If $f(x_r)$ falls between the best and worst of the *other* points, accept it in place of $x_{p+1}$: the iteration is done. 4. If $f(x_r)$ beats every other point, try **expanding** further in that direction: $x_e = \gamma x_r + (1-\gamma)\bar x$; keep whichever of $x_e,x_r$ is better, in place of $x_{p+1}$. 5. If $f(x_r)$ is worse than every other point, **contract** instead: let $x_h$ be $x_r$ if it at least beat the old worst point, otherwise the old worst point itself; contract toward $\bar x$, $x_c=\beta x_h+(1-\beta)\bar x$. If this improves on $x_h$, use it. Otherwise **shrink** the whole simplex toward the current best point, $x_i \leftarrow \delta x_i + (1-\delta)x_1$ for $i=2,\ldots,p+1$. Convergence is judged by the spread of function values, or of the points themselves, across the simplex. Nelder–Mead is the default method in R's `optim()` and is available (though not the default) in `scipy.optimize.minimize`. ### Simulated annealing (optional) Unlike everything above, simulated annealing (SA) is a *stochastic* descent method that deliberately allows uphill moves. It runs a Metropolis-style chain: at "temperature" $\tau_j$, propose $\tilde\theta$ from $g_t(\cdot\mid\theta_t)$ and accept it (setting $\theta_{t+1}=\tilde\theta$) with probability $$\min\!\left(1,\ \exp\!\left(\frac{f(\theta_t)-f(\tilde\theta)}{\tau_j}\right)\right),$$ otherwise keep $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t$; repeat $m_j$ times per temperature, then cool $\tau_j\to\tau_{j+1}$ and grow $m_j\to m_{j+1}$ according to some schedule. At a fixed temperature, this samples (approximately, if run long enough) from the stationary distribution $\exp(-f(\theta)/\tau_j)$; as $\tau_j\to0$, that distribution concentrates increasingly on the *global* minimum, since deep wells become relatively deeper than shallow ones as the temperature drops. Choose $\tau_0$ large enough that the acceptance probability is close to 1 for any pair of points in the domain, so the chain can explore the whole space initially; there is always a risk of getting trapped in a local minimum as the temperature falls, which makes the cooling schedule the crux of the method. SA can converge slowly, and multiple or stratified starting points — the usual defense against multimodality elsewhere — are correspondingly expensive here too. ### Combinatorial (discrete) optimization Some statistical problems — variable selection, notably — have a genuinely discrete domain and need different tools: simulated annealing extends directly to discrete spaces; **genetic algorithms** treat candidate solutions as chromosomes with loci, and evolve a population via mutation and crossover (useful for high-dimensional variable selection); **stochastic search variable selection** is a popular Bayesian, MCMC-based alternative. ## Optimization in Python `scipy.optimize` implements much of the above. `minimize_scalar` provides golden section search (`golden`) and Brent's method (golden section combined with interpolation, comparable to `optimize()` in R). `minimize` covers multivariate methods including Nelder–Mead and BFGS; it accepts an optional analytic gradient (falling back to a numerical one otherwise) and supports several kinds of constraints, though not every method accepts every constraint type. Refitting the Mauna Loa CO$_2$ model through `minimize` (writing the negative log-likelihood with $\log\sigma^2$ as the fourth parameter, to sidestep the $\sigma^2>0$ constraint) and comparing `Nelder-Mead` against `BFGS` across several starting values reproduces the earlier lesson: bad starting values can make BFGS fail even though the underlying problem hasn't changed. One trap worth flagging explicitly: the `hess_inv` returned by BFGS is only its *running approximation* to the inverse Hessian, not a real numerical estimate at the optimum — use a package such as `numdifftools`, or compute it directly, if the Hessian itself is needed (e.g. for standard errors). **Automatic differentiation.** From the user's side, this usually just means writing the objective with JAX, PyTorch, or a similar array library and handing the resulting gradient/Hessian functions to whichever optimizer accepts them — worth doing whenever the alternative is hand-deriving derivatives or leaving the optimizer to numerical differencing. **Practical considerations, regardless of software:** - Try several starting values, for the usual three reasons: avoiding divergence, converging faster, and avoiding the wrong local optimum. - *Scale* the problem so a unit step in any coordinate produces a comparable change in the objective (ideally close to a unit change, near the optimum). If $x_j$ varies $p$ orders of magnitude differently from the rest, reparameterize as $\tilde x_j = x_j\cdot 10^p$ (or work on the log scale) and convert back afterward. - If the objective itself takes very large or small values near the solution, rescale it too — otherwise a gradient can look converged (near zero) purely because the objective's scale is small. Working with a log-likelihood already helps here even without literal overflow/underflow risk. - Always sanity-check the answer — in particular, check that it hasn't "converged" onto the boundary of the parameter space. - It's usually worth supplying an analytic gradient; usually *not* worth the extra effort of supplying an analytic Hessian (Venables and Ripley). - Non-negative parameters (variance components, etc.) are often easiest handled by optimizing over their log. - A pleasant fact specific to likelihoods: asymptotically (large $n$) they are approximately quadratic near the MLE — this is exactly the asymptotic normality of the MLE — which is a very friendly surface to optimize over. ## Convexity Convex optimization matters because it removes the single hardest general difficulty above: telling a local optimum from the global one. A set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p$ is **convex** if the line segment between any two points of $S$ lies in $S$; equivalently, every convex combination $\sum_i\alpha_ix_i$ ($\alpha_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$) of points of $S$ is also in $S$. A function defined on a convex set is **convex** if $f(\sum_i\alpha_ix_i)\le\sum_i\alpha_if(x_i)$ for every such combination of points in its domain (**strictly** convex if the inequality is strict). Two equivalent derivative conditions are useful in practice: the **first-order condition**, $f$ is convex iff $$f(x) \ge f(y) + \nabla f(y)^\top(x-y) \qquad \text{for all } x,y \text{ in the domain},$$ i.e. every tangent-plane approximation lies below the function everywhere; and the **second-order condition** (twice-differentiable case), $f$ is convex iff $f''(x)\ge0$ everywhere (univariate) or the Hessian is positive semi-definite everywhere (multivariate) — a concave function ($f''\le0$) is handled by applying the theory to $-f$. Norms are convex, by the triangle inequality, and there is a body of results (see Boyd and Vandenberghe) on which operations preserve convexity, useful for recognizing when a problem is secretly convex. The payoff for all this bookkeeping: for a convex $f$, every stationary point ($\nabla f=0$) is a *global* minimum, with no local-optimum trap to worry about. ### The MM algorithm "Majorize–minorize" (the minorize half is the mirror-image recipe for maximization; the version below minorizes to maximize). To minimize $f$, construct at the current iterate $x_t$ a **majorizing function** $g_t$ that agrees with $f$ at $x_t$ ($f(x_t)=g_t(x_t)$) and lies above it everywhere else ($f(x)\le g_t(x)$ for all $x$). Minimize (or just move downhill on) $g_t$ to get $x_{t+1}$, majorize again at the new point, and repeat. Because $g_t\ge f$ everywhere and the two agree at $x_t$, minimizing $g_t$ can only decrease $f$ — the algorithm is guaranteed to go downhill and is numerically very stable (it cannot over- or under-shoot), at the cost of often being slow. The craft is entirely in finding a majorizer that is both tight and easy to minimize. **Worked example: median (least absolute deviation) regression.** Minimize $f(\theta)=\sum_i|r_i(\theta)|$ with $r_i(\theta)=y_i-z_i^\top\theta$ — convex, since affine functions are convex, convex functions of affine functions are convex, and sums of convex functions are convex. Write $|r_i(\theta)|=\sqrt{r_i(\theta)^2}$ and use the standard tangent-line bound for the *concave* function $h(u)=\sqrt u$, $h(u)\le h(v)+h'(v)(u-v)$ (equality at $u=v$), with $u=r_i(\theta)^2$, $v=r_i(\theta_t)^2$. Summing over $i$ gives a majorizer that, after dropping the part not involving $\theta$, is exactly a **weighted least squares** problem with weights $w_i = 1/\sqrt{r_i(\theta_t)^2}$ — intuitively, observations with a currently small residual get up-weighted, which is exactly what's needed to make a least-squares surrogate behave like minimizing absolute deviations. The update is $$\theta_{t+1} = \big(Z^\top W(\theta_t) Z\big)^{-1} Z^\top W(\theta_t) Y.$$ Caution: a residual very close to zero produces a very large weight, which can destabilize the fit. ### The EM algorithm EM is a special case of MM, best motivated from a missing-data perspective. Suppose we want to maximize $L(\theta\mid x) = f(x;\theta) = \int f(x,z;\theta)\,dz$, where the integral over the latent/missing data $z$ makes direct maximization hard. (Often $z$ is introduced purely to make the problem tractable — e.g. component-membership indicators in a mixture model — in which case direct maximization of $L(\theta\mid x)$, without inventing $z$, remains an option and sometimes works better.) Define $$Q(\theta\mid\theta^t) = E\big[\log L(\theta\mid Y) \mid x;\theta^t\big],$$ the expectation taken with respect to $z\mid x,\theta^t$. The algorithm: 1. **E step**: compute $Q(\theta\mid\theta^t)$, ideally in closed form. 2. **M step**: maximize $Q(\theta\mid\theta^t)$ over $\theta$ to get $\theta^{t+1}$ (falling back to a numerical method above if this isn't closed-form either). 3. Repeat to convergence. When the E step has no closed form, one standard fallback is Monte Carlo (draw $z_j$ from $f(z\mid x,\theta^t)$, average $\log f(x,z_j;\theta)$ over the draws) — Monte Carlo EM, which tends to be much slower; EM can be slow even when the E step is exact. EM increases the objective at every step (provable via Jensen's inequality — equivalently the information inequality for Kullback–Leibler divergence; see Givens and Hoeting, p. 95); equivalently, at each step it maximizes a *minorizing* function for $\log L(\theta)$ that is tangent to it at $\theta^t$ and lies below it everywhere — the MM idea, for maximization. **Worked example: a Gaussian mixture.** $f(x;\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k f_k(x;\mu_k,\sigma_k)$, $\theta=\{\{\pi_k\},\{\mu_k\},\{\sigma_k\}\}$. The likelihood is a product (over observations) of a sum (over components) and is well known to be multimodal (label switching). Take the component membership $z_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ as the missing data — introducing it "breaks the mixture": *if* every $z_i$ were known, estimating each component's parameters from its own observations would be easy (an ordinary sample mean and variance, for a Gaussian component). EM produces a "soft", probability-weighted version of exactly that. The E step needs $p_{ik}^t = \Pr(z_i=k\mid x_i;\theta^t)$, obtained from Bayes' theorem, $$p_{ik}^t = \frac{\pi_k^t f_k(x_i;\mu_k^t,\sigma_k^t)}{\sum_j \pi_j^t f_j(x_i;\mu_j^t,\sigma_j^t)},$$ after which $Q(\theta\mid\theta^t)=\sum_i\sum_k p_{ik}^t\big(\log f_k(x_i;\mu_k,\sigma_k)+\log\pi_k\big)$ splits cleanly into a term in the component parameters and a term in the mixture weights, each maximized separately in the M step — for Gaussian components, the updates are just the $p_{ik}^t$-weighted sample mean and variance within each component. ## Optimization under constraints Constrained optimization is harder than unconstrained; inequality constraints are harder than equality constraints. Where possible, sidestep the issue by reparameterizing instead: optimize a non-negative parameter (a variance component) on the log scale, or a parameter confined to $(0,1)$ (or any bounded interval, after rescaling) via a logit transform. The general vocabulary is "programming": different objective/constraint combinations give **linear**, **quadratic**, **second-order cone**, and **semidefinite** programming, in roughly increasing order of computational difficulty, all special cases of **convex programming**, $$\min_x f(x) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad h_j(x)\le0\ (j=1,\ldots,m), \quad a_i^\top x = b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,q),$$ with $f$ and every $h_j$ convex. (An equality $g(x)=b$ can always be written as the pair $g(x)\le b$, $g(x)\ge b$; a $\ge$ inequality becomes $\le$ by negating it.) An $x$ satisfying every constraint is **feasible**. Good, scalable algorithms exist for convex programs; the main practical difficulty is usually *recognizing* (or engineering, by reformulation) that a problem is one. **Linear programming**: minimize $c^\top x$ subject to $Ax\preceq b$ (a system of half-space constraints, one per row). The minimum of a linear objective over a polyhedron occurs at a vertex, so the simplex method starts at a feasible vertex and walks along edges that improve the objective; interior-point methods are the other standard family. ### Equality-constrained problems **Linear equality constraints**, $Ax=b$: reduce to an unconstrained problem in fewer variables. Given one feasible point $x_c$ (e.g. $x_c=A^+b$ via the pseudoinverse) and a basis $B$ for the null space of $A$ (from the SVD of $A$: the columns of $V$ with zero singular value; or from the QR decomposition of $A^\top$), every feasible $x$ is $x_c+Bz$ for some $z\in\mathbb{R}^{p-q}$. Minimizing $h(z)=f(x_c+Bz)$ — an ordinary unconstrained problem in $p-q$ variables, with $\nabla h(z)=B^\top\nabla f(x_c+Bz)$ and $H_h(z)=B^\top H_f(x_c+Bz)B$ — solves the original problem. **Nonlinear equality constraints**, $g_i(x)=b_i$: use a Lagrange multiplier, forming $L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^\top(g(x)-b)$; setting $\nabla_{x,\lambda}L=0$ gives a critical point of $f$ that also satisfies the constraints. **Worked example: equality-constrained quadratic programming.** Minimize $f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Qx+m^\top x+c$ ($Q$ positive semi-definite) subject to $Ax=b$. The Lagrangian gives $\nabla_xL=m+Qx+A^\top\lambda=0$ together with $Ax=b$, i.e. the linear system $$\begin{pmatrix}Q & A^\top\\ A & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x\\ \lambda\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-m\\ b\end{pmatrix},$$ solvable directly, or, via block-matrix inverse formulas, $x^{*} = -Q^{-1}m + Q^{-1}A^\top(AQ^{-1}A^\top)^{-1}(AQ^{-1}m+b)$. ### The Lagrangian dual (optional) With equality constraints $g_i(x)=0$ and inequalities $h_j(x)\le0$, form $$L(x,\lambda,\mu) = f(x) + \sum_i\lambda_ig_i(x) + \sum_j\mu_jh_j(x),$$ and note that $\inf_x\sup_{\lambda,\mu:\mu\succeq0}L(x,\lambda,\mu)$ recovers the original problem, because the inner supremum is $+\infty$ at any infeasible $x$. Swapping the order of $\inf$ and $\sup$ can only decrease the value (**weak duality**): $$\sup_{\lambda,\mu\succeq0}\inf_x L(x,\lambda,\mu) \;\le\; \inf_x\sup_{\lambda,\mu\succeq0} L(x,\lambda,\mu).$$ The left side, with the inner infimum evaluated, defines the **dual function** $d(\lambda,\mu)=\inf_xL(x,\lambda,\mu)$ — always concave, being a pointwise infimum of affine functions of $(\lambda,\mu)$ — and the **dual problem** is $\sup_{\lambda,\mu\succeq0}d(\lambda,\mu)$, always a convex optimization problem regardless of whether the primal is. When the primal and dual optima differ, there is a **duality gap**; for convex programs satisfying mild *constraint qualifications* (the usual case), there is none, so solving the — sometimes much easier — dual solves the primal. At the optimum, $\mu_i^{*}=0$ unless the $i$-th inequality is *active*, and $x^{*}$ minimizes $L(x,\lambda^{*},\mu^{*})$, so once $(\lambda^{*},\mu^{*})$ is known, what remains is an unconstrained convex minimization. **Worked example.** Minimize $x^\top x$ s.t. $Ax=b$. $L(x,\lambda)=x^\top x+\lambda^\top(Ax-b)$; $\nabla_xL=2x+A^\top\lambda=0 \Rightarrow x=-\tfrac12A^\top\lambda$; substituting back gives the concave quadratic dual $d(\lambda)=-\tfrac14\lambda^\top AA^\top\lambda-b^\top\lambda$, an unconstrained problem in $\lambda$ that recovers $x^{*}$. (The primal and dual forms of the SVM classifier tell a similar story: the primal optimizes over $\mathbb{R}^p$, the dual over $\mathbb{R}^n$, so the dual is the better choice when $n\ll p$.) ### KKT conditions (optional) The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions generalize the Lagrange-multiplier picture to include inequalities. With $f,g_i,h_j$ continuously differentiable near $x^{*}$: if $x^{*}$ and $(\lambda^{*},\mu^{*})$ are primal/dual optimal and there is no duality gap, then $$h_j(x^{*})\le0,\qquad g_i(x^{*})=0,\qquad \mu_j^{*}\ge0,\qquad \mu_j^{*}h_j(x^{*})=0,$$ $$\nabla f(x^{*}) + \sum_i\lambda_i^{*}\nabla g_i(x^{*}) + \sum_j\mu_j^{*}\nabla h_j(x^{*}) = 0,$$ and for convex problems these conditions are also *sufficient*: any point satisfying them is primal/dual optimal with no duality gap. A second-order refinement, for checking a specific candidate $x^{*}$: call $w$ a **tangent direction** with respect to a constraint $g_i$ if $\nabla g_i(x)^\top w=0$ — moving along $w$ from a point on the constraint surface keeps you on it, the only legitimate direction to move in. If the Lagrangian's gradient vanishes at $x^{*}$ and $w^\top H_L(x^{*},\lambda,\mu)w>0$ for every tangent direction $w$ with respect to the equality constraints and every *active* inequality constraint ($h_j(x^{*})=0$), then $x^{*}$ is a local minimum — the Hessian only needs to be positive in the directions one is actually allowed to move in, weaker than positive definiteness everywhere. ### Interior-point (barrier) methods Newton's method already handles linear equality constraints directly (see above), so one standard strategy for the general convex program folds the inequality constraints into the objective instead, via an indicator $I_-(u)=0$ if $u\le0$, $\infty$ otherwise: $$f(x) + \sum_{j=1}^m I_-(h_j(x)).$$ This isn't differentiable, so replace the indicator with a smooth **log barrier**, $$\tilde f(x) = f(x) - \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{1}{t}\log(-h_j(x)),$$ convex and differentiable, increasingly steep near the boundary of the feasible region as $t\to\infty$. Run Newton's method (with only the linear equality constraints) on $\tilde f$, letting $t$ grow across iterations so the solution can approach the boundary if that's where the true optimum lies. Each Newton step — starting from a feasible $x_0$ (i.e. $Ax_0=b$) and requiring every step to preserve feasibility, $A(x_{t+1}-x_t)=0$ — solves $$\begin{pmatrix}H_{\tilde f}(x_t) & A^\top\\ A & 0\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}x_{t+1}-x_t\\ \lambda\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-\nabla\tilde f(x_t)\\ 0\end{pmatrix},$$ the same block system as the equality-constrained QP above, because the whole idea is again to substitute a quadratic approximation (here, of $\tilde f$) for the real objective. **Software.** `cvxopt` in Python handles general convex programs (`cvxopt.solvers.cp`, plus solvers specialized to particular problem classes); comparable tools elsewhere include MATLAB's `fmincon` and CVX, and R's `CVXR`. ## Comparing the methods Per Lange: MM and EM are numerically stable and simple to reason about, but can converge very slowly; Newton's method converges very fast but is fragile (it needs good starting values, a well-behaved Hessian, and correct derivatives); quasi-Newton methods sit in between on both counts. Convex optimization generally enters the picture once constraints are involved. One general caution about constrained optimization: it hands you a point estimate, but quantifying uncertainty around it is harder than in the unconstrained case. One workable strategy is to drop the inactive inequality constraints, reparameterize using the active equality constraints to get an unconstrained problem in a lower-dimensional space, and estimate the information matrix from the Hessian there, as usual. ## Sources All mathematical content is from the STAT 243 (UC Berkeley, "Introduction to Statistical Computing") Unit 11 notes, "Optimization" (Chris Paciorek), fall-2024 offering — identical in content to the fall-2025 offering, so cited once: - Notation and setup — `units/unit11-optim/01-1-notation.md`, `02-2-overview.md`. - Univariate optimization and convergence — `03-3-univariate-function-optimization.md`, `04-4-convergence-ideas.md` (golden section, bisection, Newton–Raphson and its failure modes, convergence metrics, the Rastrigin function, order-of-convergence derivation for N–R). - Multivariate optimization — `05-5-multivariate-optimization.md` (profiling, multivariate N–R and the Mauna Loa CO$_2$ example, Fisher scoring, IRLS, descent methods, BFGS, SGD, coordinate descent and the lasso, Nelder–Mead, simulated annealing, combinatorial optimization). - Optimization in Python — `06-6-basic-optimization-in-python.md` (`scipy.optimize`, automatic differentiation, practical considerations). - Convexity, MM, and EM — `07-8-convexity.md`. - Constrained and convex optimization — `08-9-optimization-under-constraints.md` (programming taxonomy, equality constraints, Lagrangian duality, KKT conditions, interior-point/barrier method, and the closing comparison of methods, originally the notes' own "Section 10 Summary").
